title: Waiting on I/O
lede: A marble reaches a point where it needs something from outside, a network response say, and cannot go on until it arrives. It leaves the running platform and another marble runs. Toggle the runtime. The scene keeps going.
misconception: My three tasks run at the same time. In asyncio and in Python threads, exactly one marble is ever on the platform. Progress comes from waits overlapping, never from runs overlapping. Go and tokio widen the platform, and even there marbles queue when the slots are full.
look: Stare at the beat where a reply lands while every slot is taken. The gate turns red and the lift holds. What separates the runtimes on this track is how many slots the platform has, how heavy the marbles are, and whether a lock changes hands.

threads.label: Python threads
threads.note: One slot because there is one lock. The padlock is the GIL and only its holder runs Python.

marble: an operating-system thread running Python code. It is heavy because the OS gives each one its own stack.
slot: the Global Interpreter Lock. Only the thread holding it runs Python code, so there is one slot however many threads exist.
lift: the operating system decides which thread runs. Python only decides who holds the GIL.
trap: a blocking call such as a socket read lets go of the GIL while it waits, so another thread can take it.
ready: the OS marks the thread ready. It still has to get the GIL back before it runs Python.
run: this thread is the one running Python right now.
token: the GIL, drawn as a lock. The marble carrying it is the one running Python. It hands the lock back to the hook when it blocks, and the next marble takes it on the way up.
memory: every thread reads and writes the same objects. The GIL keeps the interpreter safe while they do. Your own data still needs your own locks.

asyncio.label: Python asyncio
asyncio.note: One slot and no lock. The loop just runs the next ready task. Same schedule as threads here, but nothing is handed around.

marble: a coroutine wrapped so the event loop can schedule it. It is light because it is just a Python object.
slot: one event loop on one thread runs one task at a time.
lift: picks the next ready task, but only when the running task hands control back.
trap: the task suspends itself here and gives control to the loop.
ready: the awaited future resolved. The task is queued for the loop.
run: the loop is executing this task's next step.
token: there is nothing to hand around. The loop runs one task, and when that task awaits, the loop runs the next ready one.
memory: every task lives on one thread with one heap. A task hands an object to another for free, and nothing else runs until it awaits.

go.label: Go
go.note: Two slots. Two goroutines run at the same instant, one per P.

marble: a function the Go runtime schedules. It is light because it starts with a tiny stack.
slot: a processor, the scheduling context a goroutine must hold to run. There are GOMAXPROCS of them, one per core by default, and two are drawn here.
lift: Go's own scheduler moves goroutines onto Ps, independently of the operating system.
trap: the goroutine is parked while the netpoller waits for the reply. Its P is free for another goroutine.
ready: the reply arrived and the goroutine is queued for a P.
run: this goroutine holds a P and is executing.
token: a P is a slot, not a lock. Two goroutines run at the same instant.
memory: goroutines share one address space. Go's advice is to share memory by communicating over channels, but nothing stops a plain write.

tokio.label: Rust tokio
tokio.note: Two slots. Two tasks run at the same instant, one per worker thread. Same schedule as Go here.

marble: a future spawned onto the runtime, a state machine on the heap that runs by being polled. It is light.
slot: tokio's multi-thread runtime starts one per core by default and steals tasks between them. Two are drawn here.
lift: its scheduler polls tasks on worker threads. A task leaves a worker only when its future returns Pending; tokio never interrupts it.
trap: the future returns Poll::Pending, so the task yields its worker and leaves a waker behind to be told when to try again.
ready: the reply arrived and the waker fired. The task is queued for a worker to poll it again.
run: a worker thread is polling this task's future.
done: the future returned Poll::Ready with its value.
token: a worker thread is a slot, not a lock. Two tasks run at the same instant.
memory: tasks share one address space. A task that may move between workers must be Send, and the compiler checks it.

freethreaded.label: Python free-threaded
freethreaded.note: Two slots and no lock. The free-threaded build of Python 3.14 dropped the GIL, so two threads run Python at the same instant and share memory.

marble: an operating-system thread, as in the threads runtime, but on the free-threaded build of Python 3.14. It is heavy for the same reason, its own stack.
slot: with no GIL, a thread runs whenever the OS gives it a core, so two run Python at once. Two are drawn here.
lift: the operating system decides which thread runs, and nothing in Python holds it back.
trap: a blocking call parks the thread while it waits. Its core is free for another thread.
ready: the OS marks the thread ready and gives it the next free core.
run: this thread is executing Python on a core of its own.
token: this build removed the GIL, so nothing is handed around. Two threads run Python at the same instant.
memory: threads read and write the same objects with nothing guarding the interpreter. The locks that guard your own data are yours to write.

multiproc.label: Python multiprocessing
multiproc.note: Two slots and no shared lock. Each process is a whole interpreter, so two run Python at the same instant, but they share no memory.

marble: a separate interpreter with its own memory. The heaviest marble here: starting one means starting Python again.
slot: each process has a GIL of its own, so they never contend. Two run Python at once. Two are drawn here.
lift: the operating system schedules processes onto cores.
trap: a blocking call parks the process while it waits. Its core is free for another.
ready: the OS marks the process ready and gives it the next free core.
run: this process is executing on a core of its own.
done: the process's function returned, and its result is sent back across a pipe.
token: each process has its own GIL, so nothing is handed between them.
memory: each process is a whole interpreter with its own memory. Nothing is shared, so a result comes back only as a copy, sent across a pipe.
